lessonTitle: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Responses to Exercise

blocks.text: A recreational cyclist and a trained endurance athlete both sit quietly in a clinic. The cyclist's pulse is 72 beats per minute; the athlete's is 48, and no one is concerned. Twenty minutes later, on an exercise bike, the athlete is outputting far more power at the same heart rate. The two bodies have solved the same problem of delivering oxygen to working muscle, and training has changed how the heart and circulation do it.

blocks.markdown: Exercise raises the metabolic demand of skeletal muscle many-fold, and the cardiovascular and respiratory systems must deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide and heat at a matching rate. The coordinated response has four parts: cardiac output rises, blood flow is redistributed to the working muscle, ventilation rises, and oxygen extraction by muscle increases. At the onset of exercise, signals from the motor cortex (central command) and afferent input from moving joints and muscles raise sympathetic outflow and lower vagal tone within seconds, before any metabolic change in the blood can be detected. As exercise continues, chemical signals from the muscle and circulating adrenaline sustain the response.

blocks.title: Maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max)
blocks.text: Maximal oxygen uptake is the highest rate at which the body can take up and use oxygen during maximal dynamic exercise involving large muscle groups. It is expressed in mL of oxygen per minute, or per kilogram of body mass per minute. It is reached when oxygen consumption plateaus despite a further increase in work rate.

blocks.markdown:
**Cardiac output.** Cardiac output is the product of heart rate and stroke volume. During dynamic exercise heart rate rises roughly in proportion to work rate, through vagal withdrawal at low intensities and sympathetic activation at higher intensities, until a maximum is reached that is largely set by age and is not increased by training. Stroke volume rises early, because venous return increases (skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pump, venoconstriction), which raises preload, and because sympathetic stimulation increases contractility and shortens systole. In many people stroke volume plateaus at moderate intensity, so further rises in output come mainly from heart rate. Cardiac output may rise four to five times from rest in a healthy untrained adult.

**Regional blood flow.** Total flow rises, but its distribution changes. Working muscle arterioles vasodilate in response to local metabolites (low tissue PO2, raised K+, H+, CO2 and adenosine); this local vasodilation overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction. Flow to the splanchnic circulation and the kidneys falls through sympathetic vasoconstriction. Skin flow rises as exercise continues, to lose heat. Cerebral flow is maintained and coronary flow rises to match the increased work of the heart. Because muscle resistance falls so much, total peripheral resistance falls, so mean arterial pressure rises only modestly while cardiac output rises greatly.

rows: Local metabolic vasodilation overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction

blocks.title: Cardiac output at rest and in exercise
blocks.prompt: At rest a man has HR 70 beats per minute and SV 75 mL. During hard exercise HR is 170 and SV is 120 mL. Calculate cardiac output at each, and the fold increase.

steps.text: Of this rise, heart rate rose 2.4-fold (170 / 70) and stroke volume 1.6-fold (120 / 75).

blocks.answer: Cardiac output rises from about 5.3 to 20.4 L/min, about four-fold; heart rate contributes more than stroke volume.

blocks.markdown: **Ventilation.** Minute ventilation rises from about 6 L/min at rest to well over 100 L/min in maximal exercise, through increases in both tidal volume and respiratory rate. The increase begins abruptly with central command and signals from limb movement, then rises more gradually with the metabolic demand. In moderate exercise arterial PO2 and PCO2 stay close to their resting values, even though oxygen consumption and CO2 production have increased many-fold, which shows that ventilation is tightly matched to metabolism. The exact mechanism of this matching is not fully understood, and circulating chemoreceptor stimuli alone do not explain it. In heavy exercise, lactic acid accumulates and the resulting acidaemia provides an extra stimulus to ventilation, and PaCO2 may fall.

blocks.caption: Fick principle. VO2 = oxygen uptake (mL/min); Q = cardiac output (L/min); CaO2 and CvO2 = arterial and mixed venous oxygen content (mL O2 per L of blood). The difference is the arteriovenous oxygen difference.

blocks.title: Using the Fick principle to find oxygen uptake
blocks.prompt: At maximal exercise a 70 kg man has a cardiac output of 20 L/min, an arterial oxygen content of 200 mL per L and a mixed venous oxygen content of 50 mL per L. Calculate VO2 in mL/min and mL/kg/min.

steps.text: Arteriovenous O2 difference = 200 - 50 = 150 mL O2 per L of blood.

blocks.answer: VO2 is 3000 mL/min, or about 43 mL/kg/min.

blocks.markdown:
**What limits VO2max.** The Fick equation shows two sets of limits. *Central* factors determine oxygen delivery: maximal cardiac output (and in particular maximal stroke volume, since maximal heart rate is fixed) and the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood (haemoglobin concentration). In elite athletes, pulmonary gas exchange can also become limiting. *Peripheral* factors determine extraction: muscle capillary density, mitochondrial content and enzyme capacity set how much oxygen is removed from the blood. In most healthy people, the main limit to VO2max is maximal cardiac output, that is, the capacity of the heart to deliver oxygen.

**Training and resting heart rate.** Endurance training lowers resting heart rate. Training raises vagal (parasympathetic) tone and lowers intrinsic sinoatrial node rate, so heart rate falls at rest. Training also increases stroke volume through a larger ventricular cavity (with increased ventricular mass), greater filling and stronger contraction. Because cardiac output at rest is largely unchanged, a larger stroke volume allows the same output at a lower rate. Maximal heart rate does not rise with training; maximal cardiac output rises because stroke volume rises.

items: Cardiac output rises four to five-fold in untrained adults, from both heart rate and stroke volume.
Blood is redistributed: muscle and coronary flow increase, splanchnic and renal flow decrease, cerebral flow is maintained, and skin flow rises to lose heat.
Ventilation rises abruptly and then progressively, matching oxygen consumption, so arterial PO2 and PCO2 are held near resting values in moderate exercise.
VO2max = maximal cardiac output x maximal arteriovenous O2 difference (Fick).
Training lowers resting heart rate through more vagal tone and a larger stroke volume, and raises VO2max mainly by raising maximal stroke volume.

blocks.title: Maximal heart rate does not rise with training
blocks.text: Endurance training does not raise maximal heart rate; it raises maximal stroke volume and so maximal cardiac output. At rest, training lowers the heart rate because vagal tone is higher and stroke volume is larger.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the blood flow rules
blocks.text: Sympathetic stimulation constricts the arterioles of the splanchnic and renal circulation, but it does not stop muscle flow rising. Local metabolic vasodilation in active muscle overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction.

points: Exercise increases cardiac output through heart rate and stroke volume, redistributes blood to active muscle (local metabolic vasodilation) and away from splanchnic and renal beds, and matches ventilation to oxygen consumption.
VO2 = cardiac output x arteriovenous oxygen difference (Fick); VO2max is the plateau of oxygen uptake in maximal dynamic exercise.
In most healthy people maximal cardiac output (stroke volume) is the main limit to VO2max; peripheral extraction and, in elite athletes, lung gas exchange also matter.
Training lowers resting heart rate via increased vagal tone and increased stroke volume; maximal heart rate does not rise.

questions.stem: During dynamic exercise, blood flow to active skeletal muscle rises greatly even though sympathetic activity is high. What is the main reason?

options.text: Local metabolic vasodilation in the muscle overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction
Sympathetic nerves cause vasodilation of muscle arterioles
Parasympathetic stimulation of muscle arterioles increases flow
Blood pressure falls sharply, drawing more blood into the muscle

questions.correctOptionText: Local metabolic vasodilation in the muscle overrides sympathetic vasoconstriction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: metabolites such as low PO2, K+, H+, CO2 and adenosine dilate the arterioles in working muscle.
distractorRationale.b: Sympathetic activation causes vasoconstriction in most vascular beds, and the muscle flow rise occurs despite it.
distractorRationale.c: Muscle arterioles have no significant parasympathetic supply.
distractorRationale.d: Arterial pressure rises modestly during exercise; it does not fall sharply.

questions.explanation: Active muscle produces metabolites that dilate local arterioles, so resistance in the muscle bed falls and flow rises many-fold. This local effect overrides the sympathetic vasoconstrictor signal that constricts splanchnic and renal vessels.

questions.stem: Which pattern of regional blood flow best describes a person during sustained heavy dynamic exercise?

options.text: Increased flow to muscle and heart, maintained cerebral flow, decreased splanchnic and renal flow
Decreased flow to muscle and heart, increased splanchnic and renal flow
Increased flow to all organs equally
Increased flow to muscle, with cerebral flow falling sharply

questions.correctOptionText: Increased flow to muscle and heart, maintained cerebral flow, decreased splanchnic and renal flow

distractorRationale.a: Correct: flow is redistributed to working muscle and the heart while the brain is protected.
distractorRationale.b: This reverses the pattern: muscle and heart are the organs with increased demand.
distractorRationale.c: Flow is redistributed, not uniformly increased.
distractorRationale.d: Cerebral flow is autoregulated and maintained.

questions.explanation: Active muscle and the heart receive more blood through local vasodilation, the brain is maintained by autoregulation, and sympathetic vasoconstriction reduces flow to the gut and kidneys. This redistribution lets the rise in cardiac output serve the organs that need it.

questions.stem: True or false: In moderate exercise in a healthy person, arterial PO2 and PCO2 stay close to resting values because ventilation rises in proportion to the increase in oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production.
questions.explanation: Ventilation increases abruptly with central command and limb input and then rises with metabolic demand, so alveolar ventilation keeps pace with oxygen uptake and CO2 output. Arterial gas tensions therefore remain near resting values, although the mechanism of this precise matching is not fully understood.

questions.stem: An endurance athlete has a resting heart rate of 48 beats per minute. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Higher vagal tone and lower intrinsic SA node rate, with a larger stroke volume maintaining cardiac output
Lower stroke volume, which reduces the need to beat
Greater sympathetic tone to the SA node
A lower maximal heart rate, which scales down the resting rate

questions.correctOptionText: Higher vagal tone and lower intrinsic SA node rate, with a larger stroke volume maintaining cardiac output

distractorRationale.a: Correct: training raises vagal tone, lowers intrinsic rate and increases stroke volume, so output is maintained at a lower rate.
distractorRationale.b: Training raises stroke volume, not lowers it.
distractorRationale.c: Increased sympathetic tone would increase the rate.
distractorRationale.d: Maximal heart rate does not fall with training in a way that sets the resting rate.

questions.explanation: Cardiac output is the product of rate and stroke volume. Training increases stroke volume and raises parasympathetic tone, so the same output at rest requires fewer beats. The intrinsic pacemaker rate is also lower in trained individuals.

questions.stem: In most healthy, untrained people which factor most commonly limits maximal oxygen uptake?

options.text: Maximal cardiac output, particularly stroke volume, which limits oxygen delivery
The ability of the lungs to move air, which almost always limits VO2max
The number of red cells, which is fixed at maximum in everyone
Maximal heart rate, which rises with training

questions.correctOptionText: Maximal cardiac output, particularly stroke volume, which limits oxygen delivery

distractorRationale.a: Correct: delivery of oxygen by the heart is the main limit in most healthy people.
distractorRationale.b: Ventilatory capacity rarely limits VO2max in healthy untrained people.
distractorRationale.c: Haemoglobin concentration influences oxygen capacity but is not fixed.
distractorRationale.d: Maximal heart rate does not rise with training.

questions.explanation: By the Fick relationship VO2 is cardiac output multiplied by arteriovenous oxygen difference. Maximal heart rate is fixed, so differences in maximal stroke volume determine maximal cardiac output, which is the main limit in healthy people. Peripheral extraction and, in elite athletes, gas exchange, can also contribute.

questions.stem: At maximal exercise a subject has a cardiac output of 18 L/min and an arteriovenous oxygen content difference of 140 mL O2 per L of blood. Using the Fick principle, calculate oxygen uptake in mL/min.
questions.explanation: By the Fick principle, VO2 = cardiac output x arteriovenous O2 difference = 18 L/min x 140 mL/L = 2520 mL/min. This is the rate of oxygen uptake delivered by the circulation and extracted by the tissues at that work rate.

questions.stem: A 75 kg subject at maximal exercise has a cardiac output of 22 L/min, an arterial oxygen content of 200 mL per L and a mixed venous oxygen content of 40 mL per L. Calculate the maximal oxygen uptake in mL/kg/min.
questions.explanation: The arteriovenous difference is 200 - 40 = 160 mL O2 per L. VO2 = 22 x 160 = 3520 mL/min, and dividing by 75 kg gives 46.9 mL/kg/min. Expressing the result per kilogram allows comparison between people of different size.

questions.stem: Describe the changes in cardiac output, ventilation and regional blood flow that occur during sustained dynamic exercise, and explain the mechanisms involved.
markingGuide: Cardiac output rises (about four to five-fold) via increased heart rate (vagal withdrawal then sympathetic) and stroke volume (venous return, contractility)
Venous return rises via the muscle pump, respiratory pump and venoconstriction
Ventilation rises abruptly with central command and limb afferents, then progressively with metabolism; arterial PO2 and PCO2 stay near resting values in moderate exercise
Muscle and coronary flow increase through local metabolic vasodilation, overriding sympathetic vasoconstriction
Splanchnic and renal flow fall through sympathetic vasoconstriction; skin flow rises for heat loss; cerebral flow is maintained
Total peripheral resistance falls, so mean arterial pressure rises only modestly
questions.explanation: Cardiac output rises because heart rate and stroke volume both increase, driven by sympathetic activation, vagal withdrawal and increased venous return. Blood is redistributed to muscle and heart through local metabolic vasodilation, while splanchnic and renal flow fall through sympathetic vasoconstriction. Ventilation rises to match oxygen consumption and CO2 production.

questions.stem: Explain how endurance training lowers resting heart rate, and explain why training does not raise maximal heart rate but still increases maximal cardiac output.
markingGuide: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume; resting output is little changed by training
Training increases stroke volume through a larger ventricle, greater filling and stronger contraction
Training raises vagal (parasympathetic) tone and lowers intrinsic SA node rate
A larger stroke volume allows the same output at a lower resting rate
Maximal heart rate is largely age-determined and not raised by training
Maximal cardiac output rises because maximal stroke volume rises
questions.explanation: Training increases stroke volume and vagal tone, so the same resting cardiac output is delivered at a lower heart rate. Maximal heart rate is not changed by training, but a larger maximal stroke volume multiplied by the same maximal heart rate gives a higher maximal cardiac output.

questions.stem: Define maximal oxygen uptake, write the Fick equation relating it to cardiac output, and discuss the factors that limit it, distinguishing central from peripheral limits.
markingGuide: Definition: highest rate of oxygen uptake during maximal dynamic exercise with large muscle mass; plateaus despite increased work rate
Fick: VO2 = cardiac output x (arterial O2 content - venous O2 content)
Central limits: maximal cardiac output (especially stroke volume, since maximal heart rate is fixed) and oxygen-carrying capacity (haemoglobin)
Pulmonary gas exchange can limit in some elite athletes
Peripheral limits: muscle capillary density, mitochondrial content and enzyme capacity determining oxygen extraction
In most healthy people maximal cardiac output is the main limit
questions.explanation: VO2max is the plateau of oxygen uptake in maximal dynamic exercise, and it equals maximal cardiac output multiplied by maximal arteriovenous oxygen difference. Central factors (cardiac output, haemoglobin and sometimes lung gas exchange) determine delivery, while peripheral factors (capillaries and mitochondria) determine extraction. In most healthy people the limit is oxygen delivery by the heart.
